newsitem.title: USA: Liggett pact to aid Justice tobacco probe.
newsitem.headline: Liggett pact to aid Justice tobacco probe.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Liggett Group's release of sensitive documents to states suing the tobacco industry is expected to have far-reaching legal effects, including boosting the Justice Department's criminal probe of cigarette companies.

Legal experts said Friday the historic settlement reached between 22 attorneys general and Liggett could add fuel to the investigation, which includes a probe of whether the tobacco companies lied or withheld health information from government agencies.

"The Department of Justice is expected to receive the documents soon," a government official familiar with the criminal probe told Reuters. Other sources speculated the department may have already received them.
"The settlement and its disclosures are expected to further boost the investigation and contribute new and important information to the grand jury." the government official said.
He added that while no criminal charges are expected soon, it is believed indictments will be issued this year.

As part of the unprecedented deal, Liggett not only became the first tobacco company to admit that smoking is addictive, but also is turning over documents that could shed light on the knowledge and beliefs of executives at other tobacco companies about the health risks of smoking and whether they purposely marketed cigarettes to youth.

The tobacco companies quickly obtained a restraining order from a North Carolina state court barring Liggett from giving up documents protected by attorney-client privilege. However, attorneys general said that if it is found the papers show criminal activity, they would not be protected.
In addition, the papers will first be reviewed by judges to determine whether they can be used at trial.

"I do think it will have truly landmark impact across the board, not only for the 22 states ... but also for federal criminal prosecution," said Laurence Tribe, the prominent Harvard University law professor who is assisting some of the attorneys general.

The attorneys general are suing the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid health costs of poor smokers. While the settlement removes Liggett as a defendant in these lawsuits, the accord will not protect the company, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd., from any criminal action.

Reuters reported last summer that the Justice Department had broadened its probe of the tobacco industry to focus on allegations that companies -- not just their executives -- withheld information and lied to federal agencies.
The change in focus would allow the department to bring charges against cigarette companies, not just individuals, for deceiving federal agencies.
The probe had previously centred on accusations that the heads of the major cigarette companies committed perjury when they testified before Congress in 1994 that nicotine is not addictive.
"The documents will be important to the Justice investigation of fraud, conspiracy, perjury and cover-up," said Clifford Douglas, co-counsel to Mississippi in its suit against the industry.
A Justice Department official would not comment on whether the department had received the documents, but he played down their effect.
"We don't expect it to have a major impact on our investigation but we will pursue any information germaine to our criminal investigation," he said.
Separately from the Justice Department probe, the Liggett documents may be used in the hundreds of individual lawsuits against the tobacco industry pending across the country.

Lawyers said that evidence will be particularly damaging because it comes directly from a tobacco company and, under the settlement, former and current Liggett employees will be allowed to testify against other tobacco companies.

"This will make more of an impact because it comes straight from the camel's mouth," Tribe said. "I think that it will make a psychological impact on juries and indeed on judges that is even more dramatic than the sheer factual and logical force of the evidence itself might alone suggest."
